title: Numbers & shopping
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The price question agrees with the THING, not with the buyer: Quanto costa il caffè? · Quanto costano i libri? It is piacere's reversal again — the thing is the subject and the verb follows it — and a learner who has met that once should be told it is the same shape twice.

quanto agrees in gender AND number with what it counts: quanto pane · quanta acqua · quanti libri · quante case. English splits "much" from "many" by whether a thing can be counted; Italian makes no such split and asks for agreement instead. It is a trade, not a freebie.

euro never changes in the plural: due euro, dieci euro, venti euro — never euri. So do caffè, città and every noun ending in a stressed vowel, and every foreign word Italian has borrowed whole (due bar, due film).
A quantity takes di: un chilo di riso, una bottiglia di vino, un po' di pane. The di never fuses with an article here, because none follows it.

per favore is the everyday "please" and it sits at the edge of the request, after a comma: Voglio tre caffè, per favore. Together with M3's vorrei it is what carries politeness in a course that speaks tu throughout.
Numbers are just words and never change shape: uno, due, tre, dieci, venti, cento. Only uno bends, because in front of a noun it is also the article — un caffè, uno zaino, una pizza.

sentences.cue: How much does the coffee cost?

words.note: "How much does it cost" — and the verb agrees with the thing being priced, not with you: quanto costa il caffè (one thing) · quanto costano i libri (more than one). Learned whole.

sentences.trap: English asks how much YOU will pay and puts "does" in front. Italian asks what the THING costs, and puts nothing in front at all.
sentences.sound: KWAN-to KO-sta. qu is always "kw", and both o's are open and short.

variations.cue: How much does the pizza cost?
variations.changed: swap the thing — still one of it, so still costa

variations.cue: How much do the books cost?
variations.changed: more than one thing, so the verb goes plural

variations.display: Quanto costa il caffè al bar?
variations.cue: How much does the coffee cost at the bar?
variations.changed: a place phrase on the end, and the question is untouched

mistake.why: costo would make YOU the one costing something. The coffee is the subject: Quanto costa il caffè?

sentences.mnemonic: Count the things, not the people — the same rule as piace and piacciono.

sentences.display: Quanto costa un chilo di pane?
sentences.cue: How much does a kilo of bread cost?
sentences.literal: How-much costs a kilo of bread?

words.note: "A kilo of", and the di is what links the amount to the thing — the same di as in un po' di. Italy weighs its shopping, so this is the question at every market stall.

sentences.trap: It is a kilo that costs, not the bread, and the verb agrees with the kilo — one of it, so costa. Change it to due chili and the verb goes plural.
sentences.sound: KEE-lo. ch is a hard k, always — it is the spelling Italian uses to keep c hard in front of an i.

variations.display: Quanto costa un chilo di riso?
variations.cue: How much does a kilo of rice cost?
variations.changed: swap what is being weighed — di links them either way

variations.cue: I'd like a kilo of bread
variations.changed: the polite want in front of the same phrase

variations.cue: I want a bit of bread
variations.changed: an amount with no number in it — the di is doing the same job

mistake.why: The amount is linked to the thing by di: un chilo di pane.

sentences.usage: A market stall, a bakery, a greengrocer.
sentences.mnemonic: An amount always reaches its thing through di.

words.note: three. Like every Italian number above one, it has one shape and never agrees with anything. caffè does not change for the plural: tre caffè.
"Please" — literally "as a favour", learned whole. It goes at the edge of the request, after a comma: un caffè, per favore. One of the two things carrying politeness here; per piacere means the same.

sentences.trap: caffè ends in a stressed vowel, so it cannot take a plural ending: tre caffè, not tre caffèi or tre caffè's. Italian simply lets the number do the counting.
sentences.sound: TRE, one syllable with a close e and a tapped r. per favore runs together — per-fa-VO-re.

variations.cue: I'd like three coffees, please
variations.changed: voglio → vorrei: softer still, and per favore stays where it was

variations.cue: I want two pizzas, please
variations.changed: a noun that DOES take a plural ending — pizze

variations.cue: A coffee, please
variations.changed: no verb at all — at a counter this is the whole order

mistake.why: caffè ends in a stressed vowel and so has no separate plural: tre caffè.

sentences.usage: Ordering, at a bar or a counter.
sentences.mnemonic: A stressed final vowel refuses to change: un caffè, due caffè.

words.note: costare — to cost. It only ever has a THING as its subject, so only these two shapes are needed: costa for one, costano for more than one.
The currency, and it never changes: un euro, due euro, venti euro. Italian borrowed the word whole and did not give it a plural — euri is a joke, not a form.

sentences.trap: English says "euros" and Italian will not. It is not an exception to be memorised so much as a small class: nouns Italian has taken in whole never grow an ending.
sentences.sound: EH-u-ro, with the eu as one glide, and KO-sta with an open o.

variations.cue: The coffee costs two euros
variations.changed: the number changes and euro does not

variations.cue: The books cost ten euros
variations.changed: more than one thing, so the verb goes plural — costano

variations.cue: How much does the coffee cost?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

mistake.why: euro has one shape: un euro, due euro, venti euro.

sentences.usage: Reading a price back, or being told one.
sentences.mnemonic: euro is a borrowed word, and borrowed words keep their shape.

sentences.cue: How many books do you want?

words.note: One word for both English questions, and it agrees with what it counts: quanto pane · quanta acqua · quanti libri · quante case. English chooses between much and many; Italian chooses an ending.

sentences.trap: There is no much/many split to make here, which sounds like a saving — but the ending has to agree instead, and getting that wrong is more visible than getting much/many wrong.
sentences.sound: KWAN-ti. qu is "kw", and the final -i is a clean ee.

variations.cue: How many pizzas do you want?
variations.changed: a feminine plural noun, so quante

variations.cue: How much bread do you want?
variations.changed: a masculine noun you do not count — quanto, with no ending change of its own

variations.cue: How many coffees do you want?
variations.changed: caffè does not go plural, so quanti is the only thing showing the number

mistake.why: libri is masculine plural, so the question word is quanti: Quanti libri vuoi?

sentences.usage: Taking an order, or checking one.
sentences.mnemonic: quanto counts, and it dresses like whatever it is counting.

sentences.cue: How much water do you want?

words.note: Feminine: l'acqua, with the article elided onto the front because the word begins with a vowel. Bare acqua and l'acqua are the same word, and the apostrophe is written every time the article is there.

sentences.trap: Water is uncountable in both languages, so English reaches for "how much". Italian reaches for the feminine singular ending instead: quanta.
sentences.sound: AK-kwa. The cq is a doubled k followed by "kw", and it is genuinely held — a single one would be a different word.

variations.cue: I'd like a bit of water
variations.changed: an amount instead of a question, and the article drops away with it

variations.cue: How much does the water cost?
variations.changed: the article elides onto the noun — l'acqua, one word on the page

variations.cue: How much pizza do you want?
variations.changed: another feminine noun taken by the slice rather than by the piece

mistake.why: acqua is feminine, so the question word is quanta: Quanta acqua vuoi?

sentences.usage: At a table, or filling a bottle.
sentences.mnemonic: The article hides in the apostrophe: l'acqua.

sentences.cue: I'd like a bottle of wine

words.note: Feminine: una bottiglia (one) · due bottiglie (more than one). Like every container word, it reaches its contents through di.
Masculine: il vino. The plural vini means kinds of wine rather than bottles of it.

sentences.trap: English can say "a wine" and mean a glass of it. Italian counts the container instead: una bottiglia di vino, un bicchiere di vino.
sentences.sound: bot-TI-lya, with the double t held and the gli as one sound — the same sound as in voglio. VI-no has a close i.

variations.cue: I'd like a bottle of water
variations.changed: swap the contents — di links them either way

variations.display: Quanto costa una bottiglia di vino?
variations.cue: How much does a bottle of wine cost?
variations.changed: the price question in front of the same phrase

variations.cue: I'd like two bottles of wine
variations.changed: the container goes plural and the contents do not

mistake.why: A container reaches its contents through di: una bottiglia di vino.

sentences.usage: A restaurant, or a shop with shelves.
sentences.mnemonic: The container is counted; the contents come after di.

words.note: ten. The counting set this course needs is uno, due, tre, dieci, venti, cento — enough to say a price and to count what is on a table.

sentences.trap: There is no subject word here at all, and none is missing: costano already says that more than one thing is doing the costing, and Italian never writes an "it" or a "they" for a thing.
sentences.sound: DYE-chi. The die- is one syllable, and the c before i is soft — the ch of "church".

variations.cue: It costs ten euros
variations.changed: one thing, so the verb goes back to costa

variations.cue: They cost twenty euros
variations.changed: swap the number; euro does not move for it

variations.cue: The books cost ten euros
variations.changed: the subject written out — the verb was already carrying it

mistake.why: loro is for people. A thing needs no subject pronoun at all in Italian: Costano dieci euro.

sentences.usage: Being told a price for more than one thing.
sentences.mnemonic: The ending counts the things, so nothing else has to.

sentences.display: Ho comprato un chilo di riso
sentences.cue: I bought a kilo of rice
sentences.literal: I-have bought a kilo of rice

words.note: Masculine: il riso. Like pane, it is not usually counted — you buy it by weight, so it lives with un chilo di.

sentences.trap: The shopping is done and the sentence is a past one, but nothing about the quantity changes: un chilo di riso is the same phrase whichever tense surrounds it.
sentences.sound: RI-zo — the single s between two vowels again, said as a z through much of the north.

variations.display: Ho comprato un chilo di pane
variations.cue: I bought a kilo of bread
variations.changed: swap what was weighed

variations.display: Ieri ho comprato due bottiglie di vino
variations.cue: Yesterday I bought two bottles of wine
variations.changed: a time word in front and a counted container instead of a weight

variations.cue: I didn't buy the rice
variations.changed: non in front of the whole verb, and the amount dropped

mistake.why: The weight reaches the thing through di: un chilo di riso.

sentences.mnemonic: Weight, di, thing — in that order, every time.

words.note: twenty. It never changes shape — and it is one letter away from vento, "wind", which is a different word entirely.

sentences.trap: One thing is costing, so the verb is singular even though the number behind it is large. It is the wine that agrees with costa, never the twenty.
sentences.sound: VEN-ti, with a close e, and the final -i a clean ee.

variations.cue: The wines cost twenty euros
variations.changed: more than one thing costing, so costano

variations.cue: How much does the wine cost?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

variations.display: Il vino non costa venti euro
variations.cue: The wine doesn't cost twenty euros
variations.changed: non in front of the verb; the price is untouched

mistake.why: One thing is costing, so the verb is singular: Il vino costa venti euro. The number behind it changes nothing.

sentences.usage: Repeating a price back to check it.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb counts the things, not the euros.
